Impact

Hope4Spandana, Texas Chapter

Co-Founder & President · 2024–present

At my first big fundraiser, more than 2,000 people walked past our table in the July heat and we raised $80. People weren't stopping because they couldn't see who we were helping. So we made booklets and rotating visuals about the people in India we support, and I ran sessions training our members to connect with the people walking by.

Early on, most of our money went to medical kits that mostly went unused. I talked with physicians in India and we moved the funds to what they said was needed: a shelter, and shops run by people with physical disabilities.

Youth Soccer Camps & 1-on-1 Coaching

Founder & Head Coach · Summers 2025 and 2026

We'd get home at 2 AM from national showcases, and my parents covered every trip. Talking with other parents in my community, I realized not every family could make those sacrifices. Local clubs charge $2,000 to $6,000 in fees alone, before food and travel, and private camps and coaching aren't much easier on a budget. So I started my own camps and coaching, priced for families who couldn't afford those.

I made flyers, talked to parents at parks and knocked on doors. Parents didn't trust me with their kids until I showed them videos of past sessions. After every camp I looked at which drills kept kids engaged and which ads brought parents in, and changed both.

Building next

A personalized learning platform for neurodivergent students

I've known Yashwin, who has severe autism, since elementary school. When I taught him with flashcards, pictures and toys, lessons that had overwhelmed him at school finally clicked, and his parents drove 175 miles on weekends so I could keep teaching him. He didn't need less. He needed a different way in.

Most schools don't have the staff to find that way in for every student. I want to build a platform that does: one that tracks each skill separately and adapts to how each student learns, whether through diagrams, videos or interactives.

My research is why I think tracking skills separately matters. In paper [3], I showed that a single combined wellness score can say a person is fine while one area, like sleep, is failing. A learning platform built on one combined score would make the same mistake, marking a student "on track" while missing the one skill where they are falling behind.

Where it stands

I'm starting with the people closest to the problem. I've discussed the platform with my school district's database systems administrator, a UC Berkeley graduate who spent a decade at Oracle. She is setting up conversations for me with district officials and teachers about where these students struggle and what they need, and she will mentor me on building the platform starting in December.
